query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: The key to forming homogeneous noble‐metal high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles is that all metal precursors must begin reduction within a narrow time window (corresponding to a difference in onset reduction potentials below ~0.1 V). This temporal alignment ensures simultaneous nucleation and atomic‐scale mixing; larger potential offsets lead to sequential reduction, early‐forming seeds, and eventual phase segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: Aqueous (or organic) solution of five noble-metal precursors at equimolar total concentration with a common ligand shell and reducing agent present.
generation.intervention: Alter the ligand environment of one metal precursor to shift its reduction onset potential by ~0.1 V to bring it into alignment with the group; all other conditions remain unchanged.
generation.conditions: Inert atmosphere; identical total precursor concentration, solvent, temperature (e.g. 150 °C), and reducing agent dose; reaction time fixed.
generation.structural_mediator: Temporal overlap of individual metal precursor reduction onsets controlling co‐nucleation events.
generation.mechanism: When reduction onsets coincide, all metals co‐nucleate into single‐phase seeds, maximizing configurational entropy and yielding homogeneous alloy NPs. If one precursor reduces significantly earlier or later, it forms separate nuclei or deposits on existing particles, driving phase separation or core–shell structures.
generation.predicted_outcome: With the shifted ligand precursor (matched onset potentials), XRD will show a single‐phase alloy peak with consistent lattice parameter; STEM‐EDX maps will show uniform elemental distribution. Under baseline (unshifted), XRD will show multiple peaks or peak broadening indicative of separate phases, and EDX will reveal segregated domains.
generation.baseline: Unmodified ligand set giving reduction onset potential differences >0.1 V, leading to sequential reduction and phase‐segregated or core–shell NPs.
generation.boundary: Applies to wet‐chemical, reduction‐driven syntheses of noble‐metal HEA NPs where nucleation is rate‐determining. Does not apply to high‐temperature solid‐state alloying or post‐synthesis annealing processes where diffusion dominates.
generation.uncertainty: The critical onset‐potential threshold (~0.1 V) is approximate and may vary ±0.05 V with solvent or ligand system; the exact temporal window for co‐nucleation is likewise uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform two syntheses under identical baseline conditions: one with matched precursor onset potentials (<0.1 V difference) and one with unmatched (>0.1 V).
measurements: XRD phase identification and lattice parameters
Time‐resolved UV‐Vis or electrochemical monitoring of reduction kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the matched‐potential sample still exhibits multi‐phase XRD peaks or segregated elemental domains, the hypothesis is falsified.
